clue.text: Sell bike component on the radio

indicators.note: what goes out on the radio is heard rather than read, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a pedal is the part of a bicycle you push with your foot

explanation.surface: Someone flogging a spare bicycle part over a radio phone-in.
explanation.definitionFit: To peddle goods is to hawk them around, trying to sell them in small quantities.

clue.text: Occasionally Anthony Eden is angry with review that is redacted

indicators.note: redacting blacks out words, so the abbreviation for 'that is' is struck from the neighbouring word
an angry person is worked up and agitated, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: A former prime minister fumes at a critical write-up that has been heavily censored.
explanation.walkthrough: IE comes out of REVIEW to leave REVW, and those letters join ANTHONY EDEN in the mix. Eden was a British prime minister in the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: Every now and then is an idiom for from time to time, at irregular intervals.

clue.text: [Call about bad smell on old top]

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: to dial is to call on the telephone
BO is body odour
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Telephone someone about a pong coming from an ancient spinning toy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like part of the surface's old object, but it is the definition: a spinning toy.
explanation.definitionFit: A diabolo is a juggling toy, an hourglass-shaped spool spun on a string between two sticks, so a kind of top.

clue.text: English pub upset soldiers with endless beer only lasting one day

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the soldiers' abbreviation is read backwards
endless means without its last letter

blocks.note: E abbreviates English
PH is public house, as on maps
REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British army corps
ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: A rowdy scene in an English pub where troops drink the place dry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like the pub being turned over; it reverses the soldiers. ALE loses its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephemeral comes from the Greek for 'lasting a day', and is used of anything fleeting or short-lived.

clue.text: Make an effort to cycle into middle of Chepstow to get leafy greens?

indicators.note: to cycle a word is to move its first letter round to the back
middle points to the central pair of letters in the place name
going into something means being placed inside it

blocks.note: to bother is to take the trouble
the two central letters of the eight-letter town

explanation.surface: An exhortation to pedal into a Welsh town for some salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' suggests a bike ride; it moves a letter from front to back. Chepstow is a town in south Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Potherbs are leafy plants grown to be boiled in the pot, so greens; the question mark admits the definition is loose.

clue.text: Pools syndicate's leader hosted topless party in retirement

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is wanted
without a top, so the word for hosted loses its first letter
retiring means going back, so everything assembled is read in reverse in this down clue

blocks.note: first letter of the word
to hold a party is to host it
the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: The head of a football pools syndicate threw a topless party once retired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pools' looks like the football pools; it is the definition. S, (H)ELD and DUP are strung together and then reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Puddles are small pools of water lying on the ground after rain.

clue.text: Plagiarist's article receiving one fine

indicators.note: receiving means taking something in, so the article holds the next piece

blocks.note: the definite article
the Roman numeral for one
F for fine, as on pencil grades

explanation.surface: A copycat writer's essay gets one good mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a piece of writing to suit the plagiarist; it is the word THE. I goes inside it, then F follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A plagiarist steals other people's words or ideas, so is a kind of thief.

clue.text: By the sound of it, yes, gnome's an offensive sight

indicators.note: sound means the words are judged by how they are pronounced, not spelt

blocks.note: aye is an old or Scottish word for yes
a gnome is a pithy saying, as is a saw

explanation.surface: Someone agreeing that a garden gnome is an ugly blot on the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gnome' suggests a garden ornament, but here it is a maxim or saw. In non-rhotic British speech, saw and sore sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is something ugly that spoils a view, unpleasant to look at.

clue.text: Agent to support Frank's club, say

indicators.note: in a down clue, to support something you sit underneath it, so this piece goes after the other

blocks.note: frank and blunt both mean outspoken
an agent is a means by which something is done, an instrument

explanation.surface: A sports agent backing Frank's football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' is capitalised to look like a name, and 'club' like a football side; a club is a cosh.
explanation.definitionFit: A blunt instrument is the police term for a heavy weapon without an edge, of which a club is an example.

clue.text: Put off when a church covers up sin, being clinical

indicators.note: covering something up puts a new layer in its place, so one set of letters is swapped in for another

blocks.note: deterred means discouraged
taken as written
CH is the usual abbreviation for church
to err is to sin

explanation.surface: Someone repelled by a church hushing up wrongdoing, viewed coolly.
explanation.walkthrough: In DETERRED, the ERR is replaced by A CH, giving DETACHED.
explanation.definitionFit: A clinical manner is cool and unemotional, as is a detached one.

clue.text: Angry airmen fly public in prime locations

indicators.note: prime locations are the positions numbered by prime numbers: second, third, fifth, seventh and on

blocks.note: letters 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and 13 of the phrase

explanation.surface: Furious pilots fly commercial flights to the best destinations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime locations' reads like choice spots; it counts positions with prime numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: Ireful is a literary adjective meaning full of ire, that is wrath.

clue.text: Novice held back in ivory tower

indicators.note: held means contained within the following words
back means the concealed letters are read right to left

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A beginner kept away from the world in an academic ivory tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyro is a beginner or learner, someone new to a field.

clue.text: Exploit empty fuel vessels, say — wanting lead for electric vehicles?

indicators.note: an empty word has its insides gone, keeping only its outer letters
wanting means lacking, so the word loses its leading letter

blocks.note: to milk a situation is to exploit it
first and last letters
boats are examples of vessels

explanation.surface: Using fuel ships that have run dry, short of lead, to power electric cars.
explanation.walkthrough: BOATS loses B. A milk float is the small battery-powered van British milkmen use for doorstep deliveries.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk floats are classic examples of electric vehicles in Britain; the question mark flags the definition by example.

clue.text: Who's keeping up standard of potentially blue material with adult books

blocks.note: blue is one possible example of a colour
serge is a hard-wearing twilled fabric
A is adult, the film certificate
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Wondering who upholds standards in racy material alongside adult books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue' and 'adult' suggest smut, but blue is merely a colour. A colour sergeant is a senior army NCO rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A colour sergeant traditionally guards the regimental colours, the flag or standard, so is one keeping it up.

clue.text: See 13
President's tense after famous spy almost caught by both sides

indicators.note: almost means nearly complete, so the last letter is dropped
being caught means being held between two things
after places tense's letter behind everything else, at the very end

blocks.note: R and L for right and left
James Bond is agent double-O seven
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A head of state grows anxious after a notorious spy is nearly captured.
explanation.walkthrough: Bond's code number 007 is spelt out as letters and loses its final N. 'Tense' looks like an adjective but is grammar's T, placed last.
explanation.definitionFit: Franklin D. Roosevelt and Theodore Roosevelt were both presidents of the United States.

clue.text: London hospital describes treatment of cholera by degree

indicators.note: treatment works something over, so the following letters are processed into a new order
to describe a shape is to draw around it, so the hospital wraps the rest

blocks.note: Barts is St Bartholomew's Hospital in London
taken as written

explanation.surface: A London hospital writing up its handling of a cholera outbreak, step by step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of' looks like a link but is part of the fodder; the mixed letters sit inside the hospital's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bachelor of Arts is a first university degree in a humanities subject.

clue.text: Bob maybe putting musical on record

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting one item on another places it above, so the musical comes first

blocks.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical
to cut a record is to record it

explanation.surface: Bob, perhaps, putting a show tune on the turntable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a man's name; it is the short hairstyle.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a short hairstyle, so an example of a haircut, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: Managed business using foreign currency with banks out for spite

indicators.note: the banks of a river are its edges, so both outer letters are removed

blocks.note: to run a firm is to manage it
Co. is company
the European currency

explanation.surface: A firm run with foreign money after the banks pull out, done out of malice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' tempts a money reading beside currency, but here it means edges: EURO loses E and O.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancour is bitter, lasting resentment, close in sense to spite.

clue.text: See 16
Broadcast satire containing digs originally, on both sides

indicators.note: originally points to the start, so only the first letter is used
broadcast seed is scattered, so the letters are thrown into a new order
containing means holding something inside

blocks.note: taken as written
first letter

explanation.surface: A satirical show on air takes jabs at both parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' looks like jibes; only its first letter counts, sitting inside the mixed SATIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Astride means with a leg on each side, as one sits on a horse.

clue.text: For example, twist boxing glove on apprentice's head as initiation

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
boxing means enclosing, as in a box

blocks.note: first letter
the twist is an example of a dance
a mitt is a glove

explanation.surface: An apprentice's first task as a rite of passage: wringing out a boxing glove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxing glove' reads as one item, but boxing is the instruction to enclose the glove; 'twist' is the 1960s dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Admittance is being let in, as an initiation is admission into a group.

clue.text: Experience discrimination

blocks.note: first meaning: to sample or undergo something briefly
second meaning: good judgement in matters of style

explanation.walkthrough: 'Discrimination' suggests prejudice, but here it is discernment.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for undergoing or sampling something, and a noun for refined aesthetic judgement.

clue.text: According to terms of bat mitzvah you dress in this fashion

indicators.note: a term is an end point, so the last letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: last letters of each word

explanation.surface: A dress code set out for a bat mitzvah guest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terms' sounds like rules of attire; it means ends. A bat mitzvah is a Jewish girl's coming-of-age ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: Thus means in this way or manner, which is what 'in this fashion' says.

clue.text: Charles Schulz initially pitches …

indicators.note: initially points to the start, so just the first letter is used

blocks.note: Chuck is a familiar form of Charles
first letter

explanation.surface: Charles Schulz, creator of Peanuts, first pitches a comic strip, run on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Schulz's Charlie Brown is a hapless baseball pitcher, which the ellipsis plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: To chuck is to throw, so chucks means pitches or tosses.

clue.text: … biased, un-American ideas done when drunk

indicators.note: un- here strips away the letter standing for American
a drunk staggers about in disorder, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
A abbreviates American

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, prejudiced anti-American notions blurted out under the influence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Un-American' looks like a political slur; it removes A from IDEAS DONE before the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-sided view favours only one party, so it is biased.

clue.text: Perhaps shrug as contract dispute's ending in fight

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter
something that is in a fight is caught up inside it, so the letter sits within the word for fight

blocks.note: to knit the brows is to contract them in a frown
last letter
a war is a fight

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off a contract dispute that ends in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrug' looks like a gesture; it is also a short cropped cardigan. 'Contract' is a verb, as in knitting the brows.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrug is a short knitted cardigan covering the shoulders, an example of knitwear.

clue.text: 2 tenants go over agreement

indicators.note: the answer at 2 down means occasionally, so only every other letter is taken
going over something covers it, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: a go is an attempt or try
even letters

explanation.surface: Two tenants review a rental agreement together.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' looks like a count of tenants; it points to 2 down, EVERY NOW AND THEN, meaning take alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty is a formal agreement, especially one between nations.
